name: Subdermal implants

card.summary: Shaped implants, typically silicone, placed under the skin to create raised contours or horn-like shapes as a form of body modification.
card.note: Open-body procedure; infection and implant migration are concerns.

quick.overview:
Subdermal implants are shaped implants, often silicone, inserted beneath the skin so they show as raised designs, such as horn-like bumps. They are a body modification practice and sit at the extreme end of appearance change.

The practice dates to the 1990s, when Steve Haworth is credited with placing the first one. Medical subdermal implants such as contraceptive rods also exist but serve different goals.
quick.how: A practitioner makes an incision, creates a pocket under the skin with an elevator, inserts the implant and closes the incision. Healing involves keeping the implant from shifting while the skin settles.
quick.risks: Because the procedure opens the body, it requires sterile conditions to avoid infection, and critics call it a controversial departure from surgical practice.

lead: Subdermal implants are implants placed beneath the skin to create raised designs, often made of silicone and sometimes called 3-D implants or pocketing. Magnetic and LED variants exist too.[1]

The first subdermal implant was placed in 1994, and Steve Haworth, a Phoenix piercer, is generally credited with pioneering the practice.[1] "Horn implants" are the best-known form, giving the appearance of horns on the head.
Medical subdermal implants such as the contraceptive Norplant are a separate use of the same placement technique.[1][2]

angle.text: The implant creates a raised shape that is visible through the skin, producing the intended contour or design.

paras: The Church of Body Modification distinguishes subdermal implants, fully buried in the dermis, from transdermal ones, which are partly exposed.[1]
A surgeon makes an incision to the subcutaneous layer, creates a pocket with a dermal elevator, inserts the implant and sutures the incision, often using tape to limit movement.[1]
No studies found of decorative subdermal implants. Related research concerns contraceptive implants such as etonogestrel, reviewed in clinical literature.[2]
The procedures require a sterile environment to prevent infection and carry more risk than many other body modifications.[1]

timeline.event: Kevin Warwick experiments with RFID and electrode implants.[1]
